prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "NOVARTIS AG" (ticker NVS), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "NVS", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Novartis AG

mission.statement: Reimagine medicine to improve and extend people's lives.
mission.source: Novartis company website (About page), stated as the company's purpose
mission.plain: Invent new kinds of medicines so people live longer and healthier.

about.plain: Novartis is a big Swiss company that invents and sells prescription medicines. Its scientists find new drugs for heart disease, cancer, skin and joint diseases, and illnesses of the brain like multiple sclerosis. Doctors prescribe these medicines, and Novartis earns money while its patents stop others from copying them. It spends billions every year looking for the next new medicines.
about.customers: Hospitals, pharmacies, insurers and governments buy its medicines, which doctors prescribe to patients in about 118 countries.
about.everyday: If someone you know takes Entresto for heart failure or Cosentyx for psoriasis, that medicine comes from Novartis.

money.plain: dozens of drugs, including Leqvio for cholesterol, Scemblix for leukemia, Fabhalta, Zolgensma and older brands
a heart-failure pill now losing US patent protection to generics
an injection for psoriasis, arthritis and other inflammation
a pill that helps keep breast cancer from coming back or growing
a monthly at-home injection that slows multiple sclerosis
Pluvicto, a radioactive drug that seeks out prostate cancer (share shown), plus RNA drugs for muscle diseases from the 2026 Avidity deal

result.summary: Novartis has a real but medicine-by-medicine advantage: patents, a deep R&D engine (USD 11.2bn R&D in 2025) and global scale protect blockbusters like Kisqali, Kesimpta, Cosentyx and Pluvicto, giving 2025 operating margins of about 32% of net sales. The moat is temporary by nature: Entresto sales are halving after US generic entry in 2025-26, so the company must keep replacing patent-expiring drugs, which it has done well recently with strong launches and a lead in radioligand therapy.

pricingPower.evidence: Patented drugs carry high prices (FY2025 gross margin about 76% of total revenue), and in Q2 2026 Kisqali (+44%), Kesimpta (+32%) and Leqvio (+61%) grew strongly, but US drug-pricing pressure (IRA negotiation, most-favored-nation policy) and generic entry, such as Entresto falling 50% to USD 1,181m in Q2 2026, show pricing power ends with exclusivity.

moats.evidence: Patents and regulatory exclusivity on brands like Kisqali and Kesimpta (US protection into 2031) and Cosentyx (US 2029) are the core of the moat; the Novartis name itself matters mostly to doctors and payers, not patients.

Patients stable on chronic therapies like Kesimpta or Cosentyx and doctors familiar with them are slow to switch, but payers can force switches to cheaper alternatives once rivals or biosimilars arrive.
A medicine does not become more valuable to one patient because others use it.

With USD 54.5bn of 2025 net sales and USD 11.2bn of R&D, Novartis can fund global Phase III trials, launches in 118 countries and multi-billion acquisitions (Avidity, about USD 12bn, closed 2026) that small biotechs cannot.
Some niches, such as radioligand therapy with its specialised isotope supply and manufacturing, support few players, but most of its markets have several large competitors.
Its 'pure-play innovative medicines' focus after spinning off Alcon (2019) and Sandoz (2023) differentiates its portfolio, but rivals can and do copy the strategy.
It built industrial-scale radioligand production (Pluvicto, Lutathera) and gene therapy (Zolgensma) manufacturing that few rivals have matched.
Its patent estate and pipeline of 30+ potential high-value assets, including Avidity's RNA platform and pelacarsen for Lp(a), are exclusive assets for their patent lives.

customers.evidence: Physicians repeatedly prescribe its leading brands (Kisqali gained share in early breast cancer, with H1 2026 sales up 51%), but payers and patients have no brand loyalty once cheaper generics arrive, as Entresto's 46% H1 2026 drop shows.

talent.evidence: About 75,000 employees and a long-standing reputation in Basel and Cambridge, MA research hubs let it hire top scientists; it ranked first in the 2024 Access to Medicine Index, which helps its purpose-driven employer brand.

product.evidence: Several products are class leaders: Kisqali has overall-survival data in metastatic breast cancer and is the only CDK4/6 inhibitor approved for a broad early-breast-cancer population, Pluvicto was the first PSMA radioligand therapy, and Rhapsido is the first approved BTK inhibitor for chronic spontaneous urticaria.

competitors.name: Roche
competitors.note: Oncology (breast cancer), multiple sclerosis (Ocrevus vs Kesimpta), immunology and neuroscience; Swiss arch-rival.

competitors.name: AstraZeneca
competitors.note: Breast cancer, cardiovascular/renal (Farxiga alongside Entresto) and immunology.

competitors.name: Eli Lilly
competitors.note: Breast cancer (Verzenio vs Kisqali), immunology (Taltz vs Cosentyx), radioligands and cardiometabolic.

competitors.name: Pfizer
competitors.note: Breast cancer (Ibrance vs Kisqali), oncology and cardiovascular.

competitors.name: Johnson & Johnson
competitors.note: Immunology (Stelara, Tremfya vs Cosentyx), prostate cancer and neuroscience.

competitors.name: AbbVie
competitors.note: Immunology (Skyrizi, Rinvoq vs Cosentyx) and hematologic cancers.

competitors.name: Amgen
competitors.note: Cholesterol (Repatha vs Leqvio), Lp(a) (olpasiran vs pelacarsen) and inflammation.

competitors.name: Merck & Co.
competitors.note: Oncology, cardiovascular (Winrevair, oral PCSK9) and immunology.

competitors.name: Sanofi
competitors.note: Immunology (Dupixent), multiple sclerosis and rare diseases.

competitors.name: Biogen
competitors.note: Multiple sclerosis and spinal muscular atrophy (Spinraza vs Zolgensma/Itvisma).

competitors.name: Bayer
competitors.note: Cardiovascular/renal and prostate cancer (Nubeqa) as well as radiopharmaceuticals.

competitors.name: Generic makers (e.g. MSN Laboratories, Sandoz)
competitors.note: Generic copies of Entresto and other off-patent Novartis drugs.

threats: Entresto generic erosion in the US (Q2 2026 sales down 50%) and EU loss of exclusivity in 2028
Cosentyx US patent expiry in 2029 and Kisqali/Kesimpta in 2031 create a patent cliff the pipeline must fill
US drug-pricing policy: Medicare price negotiation under the IRA (Entresto was among the first drugs selected) and most-favored-nation pricing pressure
Competition in immunology (Skyrizi, Rinvoq, Tremfya, Dupixent), breast cancer (Verzenio, new oral SERDs) and radioligands (Lilly, AstraZeneca, Bayer entering)
Pipeline and integration risk on big bets such as Avidity's RNA neuromuscular drugs and pelacarsen's Phase III Lp(a) outcome readout
Higher net debt (about USD 39.4bn at June 2026 after the Avidity deal) limits flexibility for further large acquisitions

ceo.name: Vasant (Vas) Narasimhan
ceo.background: Physician (MD, Harvard Medical School), MPP Harvard Kennedy School; former McKinsey consultant and Novartis head of drug development

c1.evidence: Prescription pharma is a large, mature industry growing mid-single digits; Novartis leads emerging niches like radioligand therapy (Pluvicto) but the company as a whole is a big-pharma incumbent.

c2.evidence: Doctors choose Kisqali, Kesimpta and Pluvicto for clinical data, and patents make those advantages hard to copy, but each lasts only until loss of exclusivity (Kisqali and Kesimpta 2031 in the US).

c3.evidence: Novartis is a well-known name among doctors and in Europe, but most consumers know drug brands rather than the company, and it is not the default leader of pharma the way Lilly is in obesity.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'Reimagine medicine to improve and extend people's lives' is stressed constantly and backed by first place in the 2024 Access to Medicine Index, though management is also clearly focused on margins and buybacks.

c6.evidence: “Swiss, big pharma, innovative medicines”: the impression is mostly positive among doctors and investors, though tempered by drug-price criticism and past compliance cases.

c7.evidence: Its four core areas (cardio-renal-metabolic, immunology, neuroscience, oncology) are huge markets growing with aging populations, and Novartis guides to 5-6% constant-currency sales CAGR for 2025-2030.

c8.evidence: New platforms in radioligand therapy, RNA medicines (Avidity, closed 2026), siRNA cardiovascular drugs (Leqvio) and gene therapy (Itvisma) open sizeable new markets.

m1.evidence: Narasimhan set a clear vision of a focused innovative-medicines company built on technology platforms and spun off Alcon and Sandoz to get there, though it is a strategic rather than world-changing vision.

m2.evidence: As a long-serving insider CEO since 2018 he has made long-term pipeline bets, but he is a professional manager, not a founder.

m4.evidence: He promoted an 'inspired, curious, unbossed' culture aimed at empowering employees, though the company has also run large restructuring and job cuts.

m5.evidence: The 'unbossed' culture push and platform investments (radioligands, cell and gene, RNA) aim at continual invention, with mixed but improving pipeline productivity.

m6.evidence: A Harvard-trained physician who previously led global drug development, he is closely involved in pipeline and clinical decisions.

m7.evidence: He champions access-to-medicine programs and malaria work (Coartem Baby), though his early tenure was marked by the 2018 Michael Cohen payments controversy.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Narasimhan at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: He is a respected but conventional big-pharma executive without a widely known public persona.

m9.evidence: Under his leadership continuing net sales grew from USD 42,781m (2021) to USD 54,532m (2025) and operating income from USD 10,056m to USD 17,644m, while delivering the Alcon and Sandoz spin-offs.

m10.evidence: Novartis runs efficiency programs to expand core margins, but it is not known for a frugal culture.

c10.evidence: Its medicines reach about 304 million patients worldwide, including malaria treatment Coartem for children in Africa and widely used heart, cancer and immunology drugs.

p2.evidence: Discovering and proving new medicines takes a decade and billions (USD 11.2bn R&D in 2025) and directly extends lives.

f1.evidence: Continuing net sales rose in 2023 (USD 45,440m), 2024 (USD 50,317m) and 2025 (USD 54,532m), but dipped in 2022 (USD 42,206m vs 42,781m in 2021) and H1 2026 was down 2% in constant currencies.

f2.evidence: Operating margin on net sales rose from 23.5% in 2021 to 32.4% in 2025 as the portfolio shifted to higher-margin patented drugs.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive at USD 41,946m, but financial debt of USD 47,077m exceeds cash and securities of USD 7,690m at June 2026; free cash flow of USD 17,596m in 2025 covers the debt comfortably.

f4.evidence: Continuing operating income rose from USD 7,946m in 2022 to USD 17,644m in 2025 and operating cash flow from USD 13,039m to USD 19,144m.

v1.evidence: Some drugs are best in class (Kisqali with overall-survival benefit in breast cancer), but it has no single product that is clearly the best choice across its field.

v2.evidence: It ranked first in the 2024 Access to Medicine Index and has a strong scientific reputation, but it does not routinely top general best-employer rankings.

c5.evidence: Millions of patients with heart failure, breast cancer, multiple sclerosis, psoriasis and malaria depend on its medicines, and doctors would lose several unique therapies such as Pluvicto and Zolgensma.
